body_text: MaxLinear Showcases Panther to Accelerate AI Inference and Data Movement Efficiency in Datacenters at Dell Tech World ‘26 Download as PDF May 05, 2026 Purpose‑built silicon platform addressing data‑movement bottlenecks as AI inference shifts to real‑time, revenue‑generating workloads CARLSBAD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- MaxLinear, Inc. (NASDAQ: MXL), a leading provider of high‑performance connectivity and data movement solutions, today announced that it is showcasing Panther V, the latest generation of its storage accelerator platform, at Dell Technologies World 2026, May 18–21, at The Venetian, Las Vegas (Booth 204). This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260505801716/en/ MaxLinear Panther V accelerates AI inference efficiency by reducing data‑movement bottlenecks in data centers Panther V addresses one of the most critical constraints emerging in large-scale AI inference data centers: the cost, latency, and inefficiency of data movement across storage, memory, and compute. As AI workloads transition from experimental pilots to persistent, production-scale inference, system performance is increasingly constrained by how efficiently data is staged, prepared, and activated for inference. Optimized for AI Inference and Time‑to‑First‑Token (TTFT) Panther V reduces end‑to‑end latency and improves responsiveness and throughput for modern AI inference by tightly coupling CPU, accelerator, and GPU resources to keep data moving efficiently through the system. Inline execution of data transformation, compression, encryption, and integrity operations eliminates unnecessary CPU involvement and memory round‑trips, reducing GPU idle time and accelerating time‑to‑first‑token while freeing up host CPUs to focus on model execution and coordination. As agentic inference grows and workloads become increasingly latency‑sensitive, Panther‑based accelerators enable the same CPUs and GPUs to support many more simultaneous inference agents. This improves utilization, scalability, and overall system efficiency for interactive, real‑time AI services. Built for Today’s Inference‑Dominated Workloads As AI inference becomes the primary driver of production AI deployments, Panther V is purpose‑built to support the most demanding inference scenarios, including: Low‑latency inference , where fast TTFT is essential for conversational AI and real‑time applications Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) , accelerating document retrieval and preparation from enterprise data stores KV‑cache‑intensive inference , enabling reuse of pre-fill‑stage key‑value data across users and agents without impacting GPU hot‑path performance By accelerating compression, decompression, encryption, and integrity validation in silicon, Panther V enables smaller, verified data to move faster through storage, memory, and network fabrics, which improves inference economics without increasing power or infrastructure cost. Key Panther V Capabilities Panther V combines scalable performance, deep CPU offload, and advanced security and integrity acceleration to enable efficient, high‑concurrency AI inference at scale. Scalable Performance: Supports system architectures exceeding 6Tbps, delivering up to 450Gbps per accelerator CPU Offload: Dedicated hardware engines perform single‑pass compression, encryption, and checksum processing entirely in silicon, avoiding multiple PCIe pass‑throughs Advanced Accelerations: GZIP, Zlib, Deflate, XP10, AES encryption (ECB, CBC, CTR, XTS, GCM), and SHA‑1/2 hashing and checksums Data Integrity: Real‑time, end‑to‑end verification with CRC validation and NVMe T10 DIF/DIX support Software Flexibility: SDK supporting synchronous and asynchronous APIs, kernel and user space, NUMA‑aware queues, and peer‑to‑peer DMA ZFlush™ for OpenZFS: A hardware‑accelerated OpenZFS implementation that integrates seamlessly with Panther V to improve file‑system performance Industry‑Standard Form Factors: Available in PCIe and OCP NIC 3.0 configurations Powering the Economics of AI Data Centers The AI inference market is expanding rapidly, with sustained double‑digit growth projected into the early 2030s. title: Which Insurance Tool Allows Startups to Bind D&O and Tech E&O Coverage in Minutes?
summary: For tech startups, D&O and Tech E&O are the two coverage types that surface most often as blockers.
body_text: Why Standard Tech E&O Falls Short for AI Startups AI companies do not just ship software, they ship outputs. That changes how claims emerge. Standard Tech E&O policies were written around the concept that the software itself failed to perform its intended function, such as downtime or a bug. For AI startups, the software may perform exactly as designed and still generate an output that causes a third-party loss. Corgi identifies three AI-specific liability categories that standard Tech E&O policies often exclude. Model performance and hallucination risk covers liability for when an LLM provides false, defamatory, or harmful information that causes a third-party loss. Algorithmic bias covers protection against claims of discriminatory outcomes in hiring, lending, or healthcare AI. Training data disputes cover legal defense for intellectual property disputes related to the data used to train proprietary models. For AI-first startups, a Tech E&O policy that does not explicitly address these categories may provide less protection than founders assume when a claim actually arises.

title: Is Vibe Coding Safe? The Lovable Security Breach and What Founders Must Know
summary: A BOLA flaw exposed Lovable users' source code for 48 days. Here's what vibe coding security risks mean for founders and what structural safety looks like.
body_text: Why AI-Generated Code Carries Structural Security Risk The security problem is not the AI model — it is what the model is asked to generate. When a platform produces raw code for authentication, database access, and API authorization on every project, every security decision lands on the model. Models optimize for functional correctness. They reproduce patterns from training data — including patterns that pass authentication checks but skip authorization checks. BOLA is exactly what this gap produces. Authentication asks: "Is this user logged in?" Authorization asks: "Does this user have permission to access this specific object?" AI-generated implementations get the first check right. The second requires adversarial thinking that models don't apply automatically. This is why OWASP ranks Broken Access Control as the #1 web application security risk. It's predictable, common, and appears across codebases at every experience level. The Georgia Tech and Checkmarx data confirm it appears in AI-generated code at scale. The Lovable flaw was not a rare or sophisticated exploit. Any logged-in user could change a project ID and read another user's data. That is the textbook definition of BOLA — and it is the most preventable category of authorization vulnerability. How Managed Platforms Reduce the Attack Surface Not all vibe coding platforms share the same architecture. Platforms that generate security-critical code from scratch on every project create a fresh opportunity for authorization flaws with each build. The AI writes auth, database queries, and API endpoints — all from a blank state. Each generation is a new chance for an object-level check to be missing. Blink handles authentication, database access, and storage at the platform level. These are managed infrastructure components, not per-project generated code. The AI writes your product logic on top of a pre-secured layer. The authorization layer comes from the platform, not from the generation. This structural difference matters most for apps with multi-tenant data — any app where user A should never see user B's data. When the access control layer is platform-managed rather than AI-generated, the attack surface shrinks. The model builds features; the platform enforces the boundaries. See how Blink compares to other vibe coding platforms → The distinction is not a feature. It is an architecture. Building a production SaaS? Start with the infrastructure checklist → What Founders Should Verify Before Launching This checklist targets the authorization failures most likely to appear in AI-generated codebases. Authorization — the highest-risk category: Does every API endpoint verify that the requesting user owns the specific resource, not just that they're logged in? Can user A access user B's data by changing an ID in a URL or request body? Are admin routes blocked for non-admin accounts, or only hidden from the UI? Do database queries filter results by the authenticated user's ID on every read? Data exposure checks: Does your app return more data in API responses than the frontend renders? What happens to protected URLs when you log out and try to access them directly? Do error messages return stack traces or internal object data to users? Input handling: Is user-supplied data sanitized before it reaches your database? Are file uploads validated for type, size, and content before storage? Is any user-generated content rendered as raw HTML anywhere in the app? Pre-launch steps: Have a second person attempt to access another user's data by modifying request IDs Rotate any credentials or API keys mentioned in your AI chat history before launch Enable request logging so you can detect unusual access patterns after going live Review OWASP's web application security testing guide before handling real user data Start from a foundation that reduces these risks → Developer running a pre-launch security checklist before shipping a vibe-coded app Blink Frequently Asked Questions If your Lovable project was set to "public" at any point between February 3 and April 20, 2026, its source code and chat history were accessible to any authenticated Lovable user during that window. Lovable is now making all historical public projects private. Treat any API keys, environment variables, or credentials mentioned in chat history as potentially exposed — rotate them before relying on that project in production. Vibe coding is not inherently insecure, but it introduces predictable risk categories. AI models optimize for functional code — they reproduce authorization patterns from training data, including patterns that handle authentication correctly but skip object-level access checks. The risk level depends heavily on whether the platform manages security-critical infrastructure or generates it fresh for each project. Platforms where authentication, database access control, and authorization run as managed infrastructure — not generated per-project — have a smaller attack surface. When the AI writes app logic on top of a pre-secured layer, authorization flaws have fewer places to appear. Platforms where the model generates all security-critical code from a blank state on every project carry higher structural risk by design. Checkmarx identified three recurring categories in March 2026: injection vulnerabilities, broken authentication, and poor input validation. The OWASP Top 10 maps directly onto what AI models produce — Broken Access Control (which covers BOLA) ranks first. These risks appear because AI models optimize for code that works on the happy path, not code that resists adversarial inputs at the authorization layer. Blink manages authentication, database access, and storage at the platform level — these components are not regenerated for each project. Your app logic runs on top of Blink's infrastructure, so the authorization layer is consistent and platform-maintained rather than AI-generated from scratch each time. This structural approach reduces the categories of vulnerability that emerge when a model writes every security-critical layer from a blank state. Test authorization by logging out and attempting to access user-specific URLs directly. Modify resource IDs in requests to check whether you can reach another user's data. Verify that API endpoints check resource ownership, not only login status. Rotate any credentials mentioned in AI chat history. Run through OWASP's web application security testing guide before your app handles real user data, payments, or personal information.
